# Sensitive-content patterns for the Tier 1 CI scan (.github/workflows/tier1.yml).
# One PCRE pattern per line (grep -P). This file is deliberately excluded from the scan
# it feeds — it has to contain the literal pattern text, which would otherwise
# self-match.
#
# Private-network-shaped 10.x.x.x address, whole-token only (not preceded/followed by a
# word character or another dot) — avoids matching version-ish or spec-section-number-ish
# strings like "v10.1.1.2" or "10.1.1.2.3" while still catching a real IP written plainly.
(?<![\w.])10\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}\.\d{1,3}(?![\w.])
#
# Personal-machine name fragments. Deliberately NOT `\b…\b` and NOT case-sensitive -- both were
# holes, measured 2026-09-01 against a fixture of the real forms:
#   * `_` is a word character, so `\b<fragment>\b` finds no boundary either side of an
#     underscore and did not match the joined `<Fragment1>_<Fragment2>` machine-name form at
#     all. Adding `(?i)` alone does NOT close that -- the boundary class is what has to change.
#   * the two patterns were case-sensitive while everything else in this file is `(?i)`, so the
#     second one did not even fire on its own capitalised form.
# The joined form is what FreeRDP's `Logon Info V2` line writes into a relay log, i.e. the
# single likeliest thing to reach a doc or a commit message by accident. Only the fragments are
# written below, never the joined string -- this file is tracked and public, and it publishes
# no more of the name than it already did.
#
# `[a-z0-9]` rather than `\w`/`\b` on both sides makes `_`, `-` and `.` count as boundaries,
# which is what catches the joined, hyphenated and dotted forms, while still refusing to fire
# inside a longer alphanumeric run (a fragment embedded in an ordinary English word, or with a
# digit suffix) -- that is what keeps the false-positive rate at zero across the tracked tree,
# re-measured on 2026-09-01 over all 134 scanned files. `(?i)` at pattern start applies to the
# lookaround classes too, so `[a-z0-9]` covers uppercase. Do not "simplify" these back to `\b`.
(?i)(?<![a-z0-9])harus(?![a-z0-9])
(?i)(?<![a-z0-9])alienware(?![a-z0-9])
#
# IPv6 unique-local address (fc00::/7) in any textual form -- the v6 half of the private-
# network red line, which until now only the 10.x pattern above covered. Deliberately
# generic: it encodes the *shape* of a ULA, not any particular prefix, so this tracked
# file never becomes the place the owner's own segment is written down.
#
# Shape: a leading hextet in fc00-fdff (always four hex digits -- a value that large has
# no leading zeros to elide), then at least two more explicit hextets, with `::`
# compression and a trailing `/nn` prefix length both allowed. Case-insensitive. The
# lookaround guards keep the leading hextet from being picked out of the middle of a
# longer hex run or of a non-ULA address whose second or later group happens to start
# with fc/fd.
#
# Deliberately NOT matched:
#   - the range designator fc00::/7 itself (no explicit hextets follow it), so RFC prose
#     and this very comment stay writable;
#   - MAC addresses, whose groups are two hex digits, never four;
#   - bare hex runs (git SHAs, digests, hashes) -- colons are required;
#   - the documentation range 2001:db8::/32 used by every test fixture in this repo.
# Known gap, accepted: a two-hextet prefix write-up falls under the "at least two more
# hextets" floor. Real ULAs are allocated as /48 and used as /64, both of which carry
# three or more hextets and so are covered; the floor is what buys the low false-positive
# rate on ordinary hex-and-colon text.
(?i)(?<![0-9a-f:])f[cd][0-9a-f]{2}(?::{1,2}[0-9a-f]{1,4}){2,}(?:::)?(?:/\d{1,3})?(?![0-9a-f:])
